summary: This excerpt from Book 4 (part 103) is a fiction passage set in a futuristic city founded after a revolution. Valentine, a thirteen-year-old girl, is at a newly built cinema across from her apartment building, which children in the building flock to as the latest of many marvels, including flying cars, a candy forest, robot insect cleaners, and new housing, hospitals, and government offices. The narrator recalls the grey, hungry years of the revolution when Valentine was ten, and describes the cinema's balconies, the boys' spitball mischief, and Valentine's dismissive view of the revolution-themed films. The note also opens with a reflection that the descendants of the US revolutionaries now seek to stop other countries from industrializing the same way.
one_line: Valentine, a thirteen-year-old in a post-revolution city, spends a day at a marvelous new cinema while recalling the hungry years of the revolution.
key_facts: The day the siege began, Valentine was at the cinema across the street from her building.
The cinema had grown the night before and had gossamer silver supports and candy-apple red curves.
Valentine begged Mata and Popa to let her go to the cinema.
The week before the cinema, the city had clever little flying cars that swooped past each other with millimeters to spare.
Before the flying cars, a candy forest grew where the trees sprouted bon-bons and sticks of rock.
Swarms of robot insects gathered up litter and dust and turned it into brightly colored factories.
Valentine was ten years old during the revolution and is thirteen at the time of the story.
During the revolution Valentine was always a little hungry, and her little brother Trover cried thin sickly cries all night.
Valentine and the other little girls tinkered with the controls of a balcony until it lifted free and sailed under the high swoop of the dome.
From the balcony the girls could count the bald spots on the old war heroes' heads as they nodded in solemn congress.
Airborne robots silently intercepted the boys' spitballs before they disturbed other watchers.
Valentine thought the films were not very good, and the first one was all about the revolution.
The narrator notes that the US revolutionaries kept their GDP at home to bootstrap their nation into an industrial powerhouse.
The narrator states that the descendants of the US revolutionaries are now bent on ensuring no other country can pull the same trick off.
